title: Fesenjan
subtitle: Persian chicken in walnut and pomegranate sauce
excerpt: Chicken thighs cooked in a sauce made from ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses. It is rich, sweet, and sour at the same time. This is one of the great dishes of Persian cuisine.
sourceNotes: Fesenjan is one of the oldest dishes in Persian cuisine, mentioned in texts going back to ancient Persia. It is eaten at celebrations and is particularly associated with the Gilan and Mazandaran provinces of northern Iran.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions. Reheat gently on the hob.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Tastes better the next day once the walnuts have fully melded into the sauce.

content.text: Toast the walnuts before grinding them. This deepens their flavour and removes any bitterness. The sauce should be very thick and dark by the end. Keep the heat low and stir regularly.

items.prepNote: use 100g walnut halves, toasted and ground -- this forms the sauce base

content.text: Toast the walnut halves in a dry pan until fragrant. Grind in a food processor until fine. Set aside.
Brown the chicken thighs in butter over high heat. Remove and set aside.
Fry the onion in the same pan for 8 minutes until golden. Add the turmeric and cinnamon.
Add the ground walnuts to the pot. Stir for 2 minutes.
Pour in the chicken stock and pomegranate molasses. Stir well.
Return the chicken to the pot. Simmer very gently for 45 to 60 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce is very thick and dark.
Taste and balance the sweet and sour. Add a little more molasses or a pinch of sugar as needed. Serve over basmati rice.

items.fix: Toast the walnuts well. Add a little more pomegranate molasses and a pinch of sugar to balance.

items.cause: Not enough walnuts or too much liquid
items.fix: Simmer uncovered for an extra 20 minutes. The sauce should be thick and coat the back of a spoon.

items.cause: Cooked too hot or too long
items.fix: Keep the simmer very low. Bone-in thighs are forgiving but need steady, gentle heat, not boiling.

content.text: Fesenjan is one of the jewels of Persian cuisine and one of the oldest recorded dishes in the world. Ancient texts mention a version of it going back thousands of years. It is eaten at Persian New Year, at weddings, and at family celebrations. The Gilan province on the Caspian coast is particularly associated with the dish, where walnuts and pomegranates grow in abundance.
